```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
```

 *Task 1: Product prices and shipping costs*
```{r}
items    <- read.csv("order_items.csv")
products <- read.csv("products.csv")
names(items)
```

Part A: distribution of item prices
```{r}
#Part A: distribution of item prices 
mean_price   <- mean(items$price)
median_price <- median(items$price)
cat("Mean price:", round(mean_price, 2), " Median price:", round(median_price, 2), "\n")

# Prices are right-skewed (many cheap items, few very expensive ones), so a
# log10 x axis shows the shape better than a plain histogram.
ggplot(items, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(mean_price, median_price), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of item prices (log scale)",
       x = "Price (log scale)", y = "Number of items")
```
*Result and Explaination:* 
Here, the price of an item is more or less symmetrically distributed around 100 with most prices between 10 and 1000, suggesting a right skew on the raw prices.
This causes the raw mean to be drawn up from below by the media, although close together on the log scale.
The raw mean is not a representative value; the median is a more typical value; log transformations makes it easier to compare price tiers.

*Part B: freight value against product weight*
```{r}
#Part B: freight value against product weight
# Join on product_id.
joined <- left_join(items, products, by = "product_id")
nrow(joined)
# Items with missing or zero weight cannot be shown on a log axis, so they are filtered out of the plot (and the number removed is reported).
plot_data <- joined %>% filter(!is.na(product_weight_g), product_weight_g > 0,
freight_value > 0)
nrow(joined) - nrow(plot_data)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = product_weight_g, y = freight_value)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Freight value against product weight",
       x = "Product weight (g, log scale)", y = "Freight value (log scale)")

# A number to support your description of the relationship
cor(log10(plot_data$product_weight_g), log10(plot_data$freight_value))
```

*Results and explanation:* on this scale, the freight value and product weight show a positive linear association, where heavier products tend to cost a lot more to ship, as waht the trend line indicates (r = 0.4829651).
However, the wide vertical scatter around the line shows that weight only partially explains shipping costs, other factors also play a major role in this.

*Overall findings:* Across these bothe analyses, e-commerce order costs are heavily right-skewed which requiere log scale to reveal the patterns and driven by multiple overlapping factors rather than a single metric, most sold items fall within a moderate price tier (centered around ~100 on the log scale) with a long tail of high-priced goods pulling the raw mean above the median, while shipping costs increase moderately with product weight but vary widely due to logistics factors like distance and package dimensions. Together, 
these findings show that median-based metrics and multivariable models are necessary for accurately summarizing pricing and forecasting logistics costs.

**Task 2: Orders that were not delivered**

```{r}
orders    <- read.csv("orders.csv")
customers <- read.csv("customers.csv")
```

### Part A: orders per status

```{r}
#Part A: orders per status 
# count() gives one row per status; mutate() adds the share of all orders.
status_summary <- orders %>%
  count(order_status, name = "n_orders") %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n_orders / sum(n_orders), 2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_orders))
print(status_summary)

# Percentage of orders whose status is anything other than "delivered"
pct_not_delivered <- 100 * mean(orders$order_status != "delivered")
cat("Percentage not delivered:", round(pct_not_delivered, 2), "%\n")

# Bar chart. A log10 y axis is used because "delivered" is so much bigger
# than the other statuses that the small bars would be invisible.
ggplot(status_summary, aes(x = reorder(order_status, -n_orders), y = n_orders)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(percent, "%")), vjust = -0.4) +
  scale_y_log10(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.25))) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Orders by status", x = "Order status", y = "Number of orders (log scale)")

```

**Results and explanation:** The combined quantity of the orders is 99441. Almost all of them, 96,478 orders (97.02%), were delivered. The other 2,963 orders (2.98%) were not delivered. Of those, the biggest groups are shipped (1,107 orders, 1.11%), canceled (625, 0.63%) and unavailable (609, 0.61%). The smallest groups are invoiced (314), processing (301), created (5) and approved (2).

The y axis of the bar chart was plotted on a log scale. The small bars are hard to see on a normal scale with “Delivered” being a magnitude greater than the other qualifiers. The negative side is that on a log scale the small bar(s) appear to be closer in size to the large bar than they actually are, therefore labeled each bar with percentages with actual distribution.

Overall, delivery rate is very high. The percentage of shoppers with a problem at less than 3%, with most of these customers still shopping (shipped, invoiced, processing) and not failed. Only about 1.2% were canceled or unavailable (625 + 609 = 1,234 orders).


**Part B: not delivered by customer state**

```{r}
#Part B: not-delivered percentage per customer state
# Each order has exactly one customer_id, and customer_id is unique in
# customers, so an inner join keeps every order once.
orders_state <- inner_join(orders, customers, by = "customer_id")
nrow(orders_state)    # should equal nrow(orders)

state_summary <- orders_state %>%
  group_by(customer_state) %>%
  summarise(n_orders = n(),
            pct_not_delivered = 100 * mean(order_status != "delivered")) %>%
  arrange(desc(pct_not_delivered))
print(state_summary)

ggplot(state_summary, aes(x = reorder(customer_state, -pct_not_delivered),
                          y = pct_not_delivered)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Percentage of orders not delivered, by customer state",
       x = "Customer state", y = "Orders not delivered (%)")
```

**Results and explanation:** Joined the ID from the orders table to join the customers table which resulted in 99,441 rows, one per order, representing 27 states. I then took one-third of each state's orders to see how many were not delivered, obtaining percentages.

Roraima (RR) has the highest percentage, 10.87%, which is well in excess of the others. The next highest are Sergipe (SE, 4.29%), Ceará (CE, 4.27%) and Maranhão (MA, 4.02%). The lowest are Acre (AC, 1.23%), Amapá (AP, 1.47%) and Espírito Santo (ES, 1.87%). The largest state (SP), registered 41,746 orders (same rate as the national figure, 2.98%).

Use caution interpreting the high RR percentage. Only 46 orders, 5 of which are not delivered gives ERR the chance to get some larger percentage jumps when orders change. AP and AC experience a similar issue with 81 and 68 orders respectively that are never delivered and each have one order delivered late. The percentages of these small states should be more carefully taken with a grain of salt than those of large states like SP (3.91%), RJ (3.91%) and MG (2.42%).

One theory is that distance makes them. A number of the higher rate states (RR, SE, CE, MA) are in the north and north-east, at a significant distance from the major sellers and warehouses in the south-east. The longer the routes are the more opportunities for an order to be delayed, lost or even canceled. This is just one possible reason, as I haven't checked on the data.

**Overall findings:** In total the delivery of 97.02 % of orders took place and 2.98 % orders were not delivered. The not delivered orders were mostly shipped (25.8%), invoiced or processing (54.5%) or canceled/unavailable (1.2%) in total, which were in-pipeline from a generalized perspective.Almost all the not delivered orders were either in-ship mode (25.8%) or in the invoice or processing stage (54.5%) or cancelled and unavailable (1.2%) indicates a generalized view of the not delivered orders being progressed. The rate varies from state to state (1.23% in AC to 10.87% in RR) and the highest must be interpreted with caution as occurring in states with relatively low numbers of orders. There is a low number of large states with average or higher rates, such as RJ (3.91%) and CE (4.27%) that have a high number of affected customers.

**Task 3: Payment methods**

```{r}
payments <- read.csv("payments.csv")
```

**Part A: how often each payment type is used**

```{r}
#Part A: how often each payment type is used 
# One row in payments.csv is one payment, so counting rows counts payments.
type_summary <- payments %>%
  count(payment_type, name = "n_payments") %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n_payments / sum(n_payments), 2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_payments))
print(type_summary)

ggplot(type_summary, aes(x = reorder(payment_type, -n_payments), y = n_payments)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(percent, "%")), vjust = -0.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(title = "Number of payments by payment type",
       x = "Payment type", y = "Number of payments")

```

**Results and explanation:** The data has 103,886 payments. By far the highest method of payment was credit card payments (76,795, or 73.92%). Those who pay via Boleto, a bank-slip payment from Brazil, come in next with 19,784 payments (19.04%). Vouchers account for 5,775 payments (5.56%) and debit cards for 1,529 payments (1.47%). The count of not_defined type is very small, only 0.00%, so is it's corresponding bar.

Over 93% of payments are by credit card and bank slips combined - meaning that customers primarily pay with bank slip and card. Debit card is seldomly used.

This is NOT orders, it is payments. There is one order which may require more than 1 payment (e.g. a voucher and a credit card), and therefore the number of payments (103,886) is a bit higher than the number of orders (99,441).

**Part B: payment values by type**

```{r}
#Part B: payment values by type 
# Payment values are very right-skewed (a few huge payments), so a log10 y
# axis makes the boxes readable. Zero values cannot be shown on a log axis, so
# the 3 "not_defined" payments (all value 0) are dropped for this plot only.
plot_data <- payments %>% filter(payment_type != "not_defined", payment_value > 0)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = payment_type, y = payment_value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Payment value by payment type",
       x = "Payment type", y = "Payment value (log scale)")

# Numbers to quote when explaining the boxplot
payments %>%
  group_by(payment_type) %>%
  summarise(median = median(payment_value), mean = mean(payment_value),
            q1 = quantile(payment_value, 0.25), q3 = quantile(payment_value, 0.75))
```

**Results and explanation:** A box plot is used to compare the values of the payments with each type of payment. The y axis was plotted on a log scale due to the highly skewed nature of the payments; most payments are small and a few payments are very large. I have deleted the three not_defined payments, which are all 0, and can't be displayed in the log scale.

Boleto-type boxes are not dissimilar to credit card and debit card boxes. Their median payments are 93.89 (boleto), 106.87 (credit card) and 89.30 (debit card). The median is highest for credit card, and the middle 50% of payments range from approximately 62 to 181. Credit card has the highest value, with the highest possible payment of approximately 13664, followed by boleto with payment of approximately 7275 and debit card with about 4446.

Vouchers are used if it seems to be a much smaller amount. The median voucher payment is only 39.28, and the middle 50% of voucher payments are between about 18 and 80. The box with the vouchers is placed at a lower level than the rest.

Both the credit card and voucher plots contain numerous outliers that are extremely small, near to 0.01, for both variables. It could be minute residual fees payments that were received after another form of payment had paid for the bulk of the order, but it has not been verified with the data.

**Overall findings:** The most common means of payment is the credit card accounting for approximately 74% of payments, followed by boleto (19%). Credit card is also employed to pay for the greatest amounts, having the highest median and the highest payments. Boleto and debit card are similar, and work for mid-sized transactions. The smallest payments are for vouchers and have about 39 vouchers compared to about 90 – 107 for the other types of payments. Customers primarily pay in credit card and vouchers are used to accommodate smaller portions of an order.
